e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “air,” the atmosphere or open space around the earth. It names the surrounding medium in which people move, speak, or rise, and it can also describe the visible expanse above the ground. Its basic sense points to physical air itself, rather than to a person, place, or action. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in Acts, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, 1 Thessalonians, and Revelation.

This word means “lack of self-control” or “self-indulgence”: it describes a person’s failure to restrain personal desires. It points to ungoverned appetite rather than disciplined restraint. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and 1 Corinthians, showing that it can describe a condition or behavior involving excess. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

This word refers to death or murder—the loss of life, whether considered as death itself or as the act of killing. It is a Greek New Testament word with a single recorded occurrence, in Acts 8:1. Its basic meaning is therefore narrow and direct: it points to a deadly outcome or a killing rather than to a general kind of suffering, danger, or hardship. The surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to incite” or “to stir up”—to provoke people toward action or agitation. It describes an active influence that moves others rather than a quiet feeling or private decision. The word occurs twice in the New Testament, once in Mark and once in Luke, so its meaning is clear but its use is limited. The surrounding verse determines exactly what people are being stirred toward in each passage.

This word means “merciless”: showing no mercy or withholding compassion. It describes a person or action marked by a hard, unsparing attitude toward others. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at James 2:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the absence of mercy rather than kindness or compassion.

This word means “radiance”: a shining brightness that comes forth and makes glory or splendor visible. It refers to the visible brightness associated with someone or something glorious, rather than merely describing an ordinary light. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 1:3. Its exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on brightness shining outward.

e.t: This verb means “to put aside,” describing the act of setting something apart or removing it from its present place or use. Depending on the sentence, the thing set aside may be physical or may concern conduct and attitudes. Its central idea is deliberate removal rather than accidental loss. This Greek New Testament word occurs nine times, so its basic sense appears in several different settings while retaining the same underlying action.

“Ungodly” describes a person who does not honor or live in reverence toward God. It identifies a condition or character marked by disregard for God rather than faithfulness to him. This word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, showing a consistent description of people viewed in relation to their lack of godliness. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to mist or vapor—a light, fleeting substance in the air. It is a noun used for something that can appear briefly and then disappear. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 2:19 and James 4:14. Its central idea is insubstantiality: something visible for a time but lacking permanence. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is describing a physical phenomenon or using that image to communicate a broader point.

“Weak-willed woman” is the meaning of this Greek New Testament word. It refers to a woman understood as lacking firmness, strength of resolve, or steadiness. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Timothy 3:6. That single occurrence does not by itself establish every detail of the woman’s situation, so the word’s precise force there must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means a tree, or trees when referring to more than one. It describes a woody plant and is used in the New Testament for ordinary trees, including trees that bear fruit, grow large, or are cut down. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing especially often in Matthew and Luke. Its basic meaning remains a literal tree unless the surrounding passage gives it a figurative use.

This word means an account or narrative: a connected telling of events or matters. It refers to what is related or reported, rather than naming a person, place, or action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 1:1, so its normal meaning is represented by a single occurrence. The glosses “account” and “narrative” capture its central sense without requiring a narrower meaning.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to wipe off.” It describes the action of removing something by wiping it, functioning as a verb rather than naming an object or person. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, in five verses across Luke and John. Its uses include references to wiping, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. This same action-word appears in accounts recorded in both Gospels, showing its ordinary sense as a practical act of wiping something away.

Eliezer is a personal name, referring to a man named Eliezer. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke 3:29, within the genealogy of Jesus. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name itself is the clear meaning; its significance in that particular genealogy belongs to the passage as a whole. The name is preserved as “Eliezer” in the available English renderings, so it functions as a person’s name rather than a general description or action.

“Revealed” or “seen” describes something made visible or brought into view so that it can be recognized. The word points to disclosure rather than something remaining hidden; what is revealed becomes available to be seen. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice, in Acts and Romans, so its basic sense is clear, while its precise emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. It describes what has been made apparent, not the person or thing that has been revealed.

e.t: This word means “necessarily,” expressing that something must be so or must happen rather than being optional. It functions as an adverb, describing the required character of an action, decision, or circumstance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Acts 15:28. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the exact force of the word in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context.

e.t: This word means “shouted” or “to shout”: to call out loudly with the voice. It describes an audible cry or exclamation rather than quiet speech. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Luke and Acts. Its exact force—such as whether the shout expresses urgency, appeal, or public response—depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains loud vocal expression.

This word means “inner,” describing something situated farther inside rather than outside. It points to an inward or interior location and functions as a descriptive word. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Acts and once in Hebrews. Its basic meaning remains spatial, while the surrounding verse determines what particular place or object is being described. [p03:word:greek-nt:G2082:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G2082:occurrences]

e.t: This word means “to expose” or “to publicly expose”—to bring someone or something into open view, especially before others. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its public emphasis suggests that what was hidden, shamed, or subjected to scrutiny is made visible to an audience. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 10:33. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely how the action functions there; the word itself centers on openly exposing something before people.

This word means a door: an opening or movable barrier that provides entry into or exit from a place. It can refer to one door or to multiple doors, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 39 times, showing that it is a regular word for a physical doorway or entrance. Its references range from ordinary house doors to doors mentioned in teaching and prophetic scenes, but the surrounding verse determines the specific significance in each case.

This word is the personal name Jesus, and in some passages it can refer to Joshua. In the Greek New Testament, it chiefly identifies Jesus Christ as a person rather than describing a quality, action, or object. The name occurs 917 times in this corpus, from Matthew through Revelation, showing its central place in the New Testament’s account and teaching about him. Its normal function is as a proper name identifying Jesus in narrative, speech, and instruction.

This word means “fruit,” the produce that grows from a plant. In the New Testament, it can also describe what a person, work, or thing produces—its visible result or outcome. Thus, the word may refer to physical fruit or to the results that reveal what something is like. It occurs 66 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation, showing regular use for both the produce of plants and what flows from a source.

This word describes being overwhelmed by a great quantity of water—being “deluged” or “flooded.” It presents flooding as an action or condition that covers or overtakes something, rather than merely describing ordinary rain or rising water. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 3:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is being overtaken by floodwaters.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word describes being thrown down or scattered. It portrays something cast from its place and dispersed rather than remaining gathered or established. The two approved meanings, “be thrown down” and “to be scattered,” express the same basic idea from slightly different angles: forceful displacement followed by separation. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 10:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “labor,” referring to work that requires effort, endurance, and exertion. It can describe demanding work itself, whether physical or undertaken in service to others. In the New Testament, it is used 18 times, showing a recurring emphasis on work that is not effortless or casual. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains strenuous labor or toil.

This word means “village,” referring to a settled community smaller than a city. It identifies a particular kind of inhabited place rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 1:38. The word’s basic meaning remains simple and concrete: a village or small community where people live. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the term.

This word means “towel,” a cloth used for drying or wiping. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in John 13:4–5. Its meaning is concrete and straightforward: it identifies the item being used, rather than an action, person, or spiritual quality. The surrounding passage determines the significance of its use in those verses, but the word itself refers to a towel.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to loose”: to release, untie, or free something or someone that is held or restrained. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its exact force depends on what is being loosed in the sentence. The word occurs 42 times in the Greek New Testament, showing repeated use for the basic idea of removing restraint or letting go. Its normal meaning remains centered on releasing what was bound, restricted, or held in place.

This word means “blemish,” referring to a mark, defect, or fault that mars something’s condition or appearance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:13. Its basic sense points to something blameworthy or disfiguring rather than something whole and honorable. The surrounding verse determines exactly how the word applies there, but the central idea remains a blemish: a fault that makes a person or thing open to reproach.

This word describes something that has become dried up or withered. It commonly refers to a condition in which moisture, strength, or healthy vitality has diminished, especially when describing something visibly shriveled or no longer sound. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including descriptions rendered “withered.” Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being described, but the central idea remains something dried, shriveled, or withered rather than fresh and healthy.

This word means “holiness,” referring to a condition of being holy or devoted to God. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 1:75 and Ephesians 4:24, and is rendered “holiness” in both places. Its central idea is not a passing feeling but the quality of life and character associated with what is holy. The surrounding verse and passage determine how that idea is applied in each occurrence.

This word means “patriarch,” referring to a male ancestor or father who stands at the head of a family line or people. In the New Testament, it is used four times: three times in Acts and once in Hebrews. It identifies important ancestral fathers, so the word points to family origin and recognized leadership rather than to an ordinary father in everyday speech. Its exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means to arrest, catch, or seize someone. It describes taking hold of a person, often with the purpose of restraining or detaining them. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times, including repeated scenes in John where people sought to arrest or seize Jesus. Its wider use also covers the capture of individuals in Acts and Revelation. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea is taking hold of someone so they can no longer escape freely.

e.t: This word means “to fight”—to engage in conflict or battle. It is a verb describing active opposition rather than a peaceful disagreement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, appearing once in James and six times in Revelation. Its use can describe people fighting, opposing powers engaged in battle, or a command to enter conflict. The surrounding passage determines who is fighting and what the conflict involves, but the central idea remains active struggle against an opponent.

This word means “delegation”: representatives sent or appointed to speak or act on behalf of others. It describes a group entrusted with representing someone else, rather than the person or authority who sends them. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke—at Luke 14:32 and Luke 19:14. The surrounding verse determines the precise role this delegation has in each passage.

The word means a wrinkle—a visible crease or fold in a surface. It describes a physical imperfection rather than an action or feeling. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 5:27, and is rendered “wrinkle” there. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself points plainly to a crease or blemish on a surface.

Seth is a personal name, referring to the man identified by that name. In the Greek New Testament, the word is rendered “Seth” and occurs once, in Luke 3:38. Because it is a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object, its meaning is chiefly identification: it points to a specific person. The surrounding verse supplies the particular role and context, but the name itself remains simply Seth.

This word means “seed,” referring to what is planted or sown. It names the small beginning from which a plant can grow and is used in the New Testament’s agricultural language. The word occurs six times in five New Testament verses, including passages in Mark, Luke, and 2 Corinthians. Its central sense remains simple and concrete: seed prepared for sowing, while the surrounding passage determines whether the reference is being used literally or as part of a comparison.

This Greek New Testament word means “split” or “tear.” It refers to something divided or pulled apart, whether describing a tear in material or a separation between people. Its central idea is a break in what had been joined. The word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in Matthew, Mark, John, and 1 Corinthians, so its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears.

This word means “humbleness” or “lowliness,” describing a condition of being brought low or having a humble standing. It can refer to a person’s low position, humble condition, or lowliness in relation to others. The Greek New Testament uses it four times, in Luke, Acts, Philippians, and James. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains a lowly or humble condition rather than status, prominence, or exaltation.

Tertullus is a personal name, referring to a man named in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented as a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but as the name by which this individual is identified. The name occurs twice, both times in Acts 24:1–2, and the English rendering preserves it as “Tertullus.” Its precise role in those verses depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

This word describes someone or something that is opposed to another—set against it rather than supporting or agreeing with it. It can refer to active resistance or to a position that stands in conflict with another side. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Colossians and once in Hebrews, so its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument. Its central idea remains opposition: being against, contrary to, or resisting something. [p03:word:greek-nt:G5227:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G5227:occurrences]

This word describes someone inclined toward contention—an attitude marked by loving disputes or being argumentative. It expresses a disposition toward quarrels rather than peaceful cooperation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 11:16. The word’s basic sense identifies a contentious person or character, while the surrounding verse determines how that disposition applies in context. Its meaning is therefore relational and behavioral: it describes a tendency to pursue or welcome dispute.

This word means “tribe” or “tribes,” referring to a recognized people-group. It can identify one tribe or several tribes, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 31 times across 23 verses, with especially frequent use in Revelation. Its references include descriptions of Israel’s tribes and broader groups gathered before God. The central idea remains a distinct people-group understood as a tribe, whether the word appears in singular or plural form.

This word means “false testimony”—an untrue statement given as testimony against someone. It refers to testimony that does not agree with the truth, rather than to testimony merely being incomplete or mistaken. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew: Matthew 15:19 and Matthew 26:59. Its precise force in either passage is understood from the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains testimony that is false.

e.t: This word describes being in labor or suffering the pains of childbirth. It can refer literally to the physical experience of giving birth and can also describe labor-like anguish or travail when the surrounding passage uses childbirth as a picture. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in two passages in Galatians and once in Revelation. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains the intense pains and effort associated with childbirth.

e.t: This word means to cast, especially to cast a fishnet. It describes the action of throwing or spreading a net for fishing, so it functions as a verb for a physical act rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 1:16. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning is the casting of a fishnet.
